(Olivia Johnson/Special to the Daily Record) Expand By Olivia Johnson | The Daily Record PUBLISHED: August 6, 2026 at 10:05 AM MDT Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... In February, Cañon City said goodbye to a beloved philanthropist, business owner, and friend when Walter Schepp passed away. However, rather than wallowing in sadness, the community gathered Wednesday for a celebration of life at Pueblo Community College – Fremont Campus, which was one of Schepp’s most beloved local organizations. “Walt and Gloria’s legacy will live on through the PCC students’ lives that have been and will forever be changed due to their generosity,” said Ed Norden, the night’s emcee and longtime friend of the Schepps. “They will also be remembered for their humility. They sought to transform the lives of others and strengthen the town they loved.” Born in 1932 in New Jersey to a Hungarian immigrant mother, Schepp learned early the value of hard work and eventually went to college to study mechanical engineering and art. Schepp served in the United States Army from 1952 to 1955 and was stationed throughout the U.S. and Japan. Upon his return to the U.S., he enrolled at Columbia University from 1955 to 1958 and graduated with a degree in Government and International Affairs. It was in 1955 when Schepp met his future wife, Gloria, with whom he would spend 58 years of life. Upon meeting her, Schepp often described the moment simply as “Love at first sight.” Soon after their marriage, Walt accepted a position with the New York State Thruway while waiting for an appointment as a Diplomatic Officer. In 1959, he joined the United States Diplomatic Corps, serving from 1959 to 1967. With his appointment to the United States Diplomatic Corps, the couple truly became citizens of the world. During the first decade of their marriage, they established homes in 12 locations across three continents, including Washington, D.C., Dacca in East Pakistan, Frankfurt, Germany, and Edmonton and Calgary, Canada. As Schepp carried out diplomatic affairs, Gloria devoted herself to teaching, serving children in American communities overseas. Their international life reflected a shared spirit of service and connection, and they were warmly welcomed wherever they lived. In 1967, after Schepp retired from diplomatic service, the couple made their permanent home in Cañon City. That same year, they purchased the Royal Gorge/Carl’s Best Western Motel. At the time, Cañon City was becoming a hub for Hollywood western films and the hotel had the privilege of hosting notable guests, including John Wayne, Jane Fonda, and Lee Van Cleef. They sold the motel in 1972, but remained in Cañon City, where their philanthropic efforts continued to change the landscape of Fremont County. “I’d never met such a loving husband and wife,” said close friend and fellow PCC supporter Dr. Shirley Squier. “I truly believe that Walt was an instrument of God’s love…because he loved bringing people together.” After Pueblo Community College opened in 2001, Schepp quickly became one of its most passionate supporters. He joined the Pueblo Community College Foundation Board of Directors in 2005 and helped establish the Schepp Family Scholarship Endowment. In 2013, when the campus needed additional space for student study and community gatherings, the Schepps made the lead gift to launch a community campaign to construct the addition. They were honored at the Grand Opening in May 2015. Though Gloria died in December 2015, Schepp continued to make a mark in Cañon City — and his larger community embraced him as a member of their family. “After Gloria passed, we invited him to everything,” said close friend Dr. Lana Carter. “He loved it, and we loved him.” Schepp truly became the unofficial face of the college and was present not only at campus events but at nearly every community event possible. PCC proved to be one of his favorite institutions, and through the years, he funded a complete renovation and modernization of the science and nursing labs, providing new equipment, and supported faculty staffing for several years. Schepp also served as a lead supporter of Pueblo Community College’s expansion of Nursing and Allied Health programs at Pueblo’s St. Mary Corwin Medical Center. He was one of two lead $1 million donors for that transformative renovation, which opened in August 2022 and strengthened healthcare training across southern Colorado. In 2024, Walt donated an additional $2 million to establish a state-of-the-art Nursing Simulation Center at the Fremont Campus, which will serve students and the larger community for generations to come. The center was officially opened for use Thursday and was dedicated to Schepp’s memory. Schepp Hall was officially dedicated in September 2021, honoring both Schepp and Gloria’s foresight and devotion to student success. Altogether, the Schepps contributed more than $4.6 million to the Pueblo Community College Foundation for scholarships, awards, facilities, and program advancement. In addition to their support of PCC, the Schepps also donated 160 acres to the Cañon City Area Recreation District in 2016 and also supported organizations including the Cañon City Chamber of Commerce, Library Board, and St. Thomas More Hospital, while championing the arts through Fremont Civic Theater and animal welfare through the Humane Society. But Schepp’s philanthropy wasn’t the only quality highlighted during the celebration of life. For his friends, his greatest qualities were his quirky sense of humor, desire to make life better for those around him, and fierce loyalty. Carter recalled taking a ride in the campus’s bus, affectionately called ‘Gloria’s Bus’, many years ago with Schepp– even though state law strictly prohibited unsanctioned use. “That was the most glorious joyride I’ve ever had,” Carter said with a smile. “We took off onto Highway 50…drove all the way to the Gorge, turned around, cruised back down, (dragged) Main, drove by the Humane Society where he’d donated money, then he wanted to go out to the Schepp acreage donated to the rec. district…then we got shakes at the drive-thru at Sonic.” Close friend and financial advisor Michael Morton had a plethora of stories illustrating Schepp’s unorthodox but innovative thinking, including the installation of a “fish pond” at his hotel back in the 1970s. Morton shared that Schepp filled the swimming pool halfway with concrete and created a sort of “Rocky Mountain High” experience where tourists could fish for trout in the swimming pool. “This was all going great, but there was a massive flood that came down into Cañon City, and it took every one of those fish; they washed out of there, and Walt got to watch them go right down Highway 50,” Morton said with a laugh. “I remember, I was on the air and one of the big stories that year was the trout going down Main Street,” Norden added. Joan Pope, coordinator of the Fremont campus nursing program, shared one of Schepp’s favorite sayings and one most Canon City residents have heard him say: Bless your little heart. “He believed in helping others succeed,” she said. “Bless your big heart, Walt.” “He desperately cared for this community,” added PCC President Dr. Chato Hazelbaker. “What I know is the investments he made over the last couple of years will guarantee that this campus is strong for decades and decades and decades to come.” And to think, it all started with a microscope and a big heart. Photo: Gustina Keturakytė. KAUNAS .- M. K. Čiurlionis National Museum of Art presents the exhibition “Post-abstraction,” featuring artworks by Barbara Kasten, an American artist of Lithuanian origin and one of the most prominent figures in contemporary abstraction. The architecture of light Barbara Kasten belongs to a generation of artists who expanded photography into a sphere of experimentation with space, light, and perception. Her studies in painting, sculpture, and textile art, as well as the ideas of the Bauhaus, Eastern European Constructivism, modernist and postmodernist architecture, grew into a significant foundation for her work. Featuring approximately 80 artworks, including photographs, sculptures, and installations, the exhibition spans nearly six decades of Kasten’s career (1971–2026). Here, light is not a means of illumination; it becomes the material itself. Mirrors, colour filters, and geometric forms create situations where boundaries between real and imagined space, seeing and perceiving, disappear. Barbara Kasten will be present in Kaunas on October 7–10. The catalogue “Post-abstraction” The exhibition comes to Kaunas from Zachęta – National Gallery of Art in Warsaw, where an extensive catalogue was published in Polish and English. It features in-depth essays examining Kasten’s practice written by Agnieszka Pindera, Alex Klein and Charlotte Cotton, as well as a comprehensive presentation of her artworks, archival photographs, and installation views of the “Post-abstraction” exhibition. A bilingual English-Lithuanian edition will be available in September. “The Phenomenon of the Polish School of Textile Art” public programme Kasten's interest in the Polish School of Textile Art—Ewa Jaroszyńska (Pachucka), Jolanta Owidzka, Wojciech Sadley, Zofia Butrymowicz and Magdalena Abakanowicz—led her to spend 1971–72 in Poznań as a Fulbright-Hays Fellow, pursuing her textile practice at the State School of Fine Arts. “Post-abstraction” includes a sisal sculpture she made there. The programme (October 7–10) will celebrate this legacy with lectures, films, educational events and a discussion with Barbara Kasten. Curator: Agnieszka Pindera Organized by: M. K.
